## TL;DR

Fixed both round 1 review findings. A retry now recognizes an already-pushed release commit even when `origin/main..HEAD` is empty, but only when the current HEAD has the expected release subject and the remote advertises that exact SHA. Remote validation now gives an explicit gate-exit marker precedence over git-fatal text. Added regression coverage for each case. The focused tests and required changed-path check passed.

## Work and rationale

The first review finding exposed an assumption in the resume detection. The existing logic only checked `ls-remote` after finding an unpushed version-bump commit. That works after a failure before pushing, because the bump appears in `origin/main..HEAD`. After a successful push, that range is empty, so a retry after a tag failure never reached the remote equality check. It then repeated the build and test gate despite the main ref already containing the release commit.

I changed the resume probe to run whenever the requested version is already present in the package manifest. Remote equality alone would be too broad: an operator could have committed that version without using the release flow. The check therefore requires three facts together: local HEAD resolves, the HEAD subject equals the expected `release: <tag>` bump subject, and `ls-remote` reports the exact same SHA for the configured main branch. Only that combination sets `mainPushed` and skips checks and the redundant main push before continuing to tag creation. This preserves the existing safety boundary around which commit is eligible for gate-result reuse.

The second finding concerned classification order. Git fatal text can remain in captured output even after the validation gate has started. The classifier previously matched that text before it examined `[validate] gate exit N`, so an actual gate failure could be marked transient infrastructure and trigger retry behavior. I added the same gate-exit exclusion used by neighboring pre-gate infrastructure classifiers. Exit 128 without a gate marker remains a host/transport failure; once the gate marker is present, its result remains a test failure.

Two regression tests capture these boundaries. The release retry test models a pushed release commit with an empty `origin/main..HEAD`, matching local and remote SHAs, and asserts that neither build nor check runs while tag push does. The classifier test combines git-fatal output with a gate exit marker and asserts non-transient test classification. Existing tests still cover a git exit 128 before a gate and a gate exit alongside ordinary test failure output.

## Approaches tried

I first inspected the review findings against the implementation and existing tests. For resume behavior, I considered merely removing the `preexistingBump` condition from the remote probe. That would let any same-version HEAD skip checks when origin matched, even if it was not the release bump. Instead, the remote probe now validates the release commit subject as well as exact SHA equality. For classification, moving the entire gate handling block earlier would also work, but guarding the new git transport rule directly follows the adjacent infrastructure rules and keeps the intent local.

I ran the focused release and remote-validation test files before the full check. They passed with 111 tests. The required `REPOOS_CHECK_CHANGED=main repoos check` then completed successfully, including remote changed-path testing, the strict timing guard, local build and static guards, the UI smoke test, and rendered contrast audit.

## Challenges and blockers

The key subtlety was that `git log origin/main..HEAD` describes divergence, not whether a release commit was previously pushed. Empty output is the expected result after a successful push, so the resume decision needs a separate remote-ref proof. The test was shaped to exercise precisely that state rather than only an error-after-acceptance push in the same invocation.

The changed-path check ran remotely and took several minutes because it covered 158 test files, followed by browser checks and local guards. It completed without a failing test or guard. No external host release or real release cut was performed.

## Key learnings

For a safe release resume, commit identity must be established independently of the ahead-of-remote commit list. A commit subject is a useful release-flow discriminator, while comparing the full local and advertised SHA confirms that the remote has the exact tree that previously passed. For remote failure classification, explicit phase markers should take precedence over incidental diagnostics retained in a combined log; otherwise transport-looking text from later phases can misreport a real gate failure.
